analysis.one_liner: Cuts federal student aid from colleges whose degree programs don't actually qualify graduates for required licenses.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a vote; it was referred to the Senate education committee on the day it was introduced and never advanced further.
analysis.plain_summary: Some colleges, especially for-profit and online schools, sell degree and certificate programs in fields like nursing that require a state license — but the program doesn't qualify graduates to sit for the licensing exam or meet clinical placement requirements. Students finish, then find out they can't actually work in the field they trained for, and still owe federal loans. This bill would make colleges ineligible for federal student aid unless their licensure-prep programs genuinely qualify students for the exam, for the license, and for required placements like clinicals or internships in every state they advertise to. It also requires schools to certify their programs meet accreditation and licensure prerequisites, get a signed acknowledgment from students enrolling in programs that fall short, and be legally authorized in every state where their online students live.
analysis.who_benefits: Students — including veterans using GI Bill benefits and working adults using federal aid — who enroll in programs meant to lead to licensed careers like nursing, teaching, or cosmetology. They would know up front that their program qualifies them for the actual license, and schools that sell qualifications that don't work would lose access to federal loan and grant money.

how_it_helps.text: Colleges would lose all federal student aid for any licensure-prep program unless completing it fully qualifies a student to take the required entry exam and be licensed in the state where the student lives and any state the school advertises to.

Schools must also provide timely placement for academically related pre-licensure requirements, such as clinical placements, internships, or apprenticeships — a common way students get stuck even when coursework is fine.

Each career-education (gainful employment) program would need certification that it is accredited, meets professional licensure prerequisites, and is not substantially similar to a recently discontinued program the college dropped for poor outcomes; programs that fall short require written notice and a signed student acknowledgment before enrollment.

Online and correspondence programs would have to be legally authorized in each state where enrolled students live, with state complaint processes, though state reciprocity agreements can satisfy this.
The protections would reach beyond standard federal student aid to workforce, adult education, and military and veterans' education programs.

analysis.who_pays: Colleges — mainly for-profit and online career schools, but also some nonprofit programs — whose licensure-prep programs cannot meet the requirements would lose access to federal loan, grant, workforce, and veterans' education money for those programs, and would face new certification and reporting costs.

drawbacks.text: The bill is a strict federal mandate layered on top of state-by-state licensure rules that vary widely; a school offering a program that satisfies its own state could lose aid eligibility because of rules in other states it doesn't control, which could push schools to stop serving out-of-state and rural online students entirely rather than navigate every state's rules.

The compliance burden — certifying every program against every state's prerequisites, updating within 10 days of any change, and documenting placements — falls heaviest on smaller institutions and community colleges, raising a cost of doing business that could show up as fewer program offerings.

The signed-acknowledgment path still lets schools enroll students into programs that do not meet licensure requirements, so a student determined enough can still sign away their consumer protection in their own handwriting.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core promise is strong and narrow: students who take on federal debt for a licensed profession should actually be able to get licensed. The serious trade-off is the mechanism — cutting all federal aid eligibility for whole programs over licensure misalignment is blunt, and the risk is that schools exit out-of-state online markets, reducing access for students who rely on it. The state reciprocity carve-out for online programs softens that risk. On balance the bill targets a well-documented harm, though its one-size-fits-all design invites some collateral damage to access.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate education committee the same day, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Merkley, joined by Senator Durbin and one other Democratic cosponsor, introduced the bill on March 21, 2023.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action is recorded — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action — and the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 without the bill advancing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Colleges whose licensure-prep programs fall short — especially for-profit and online career schools — kept their access to federal student aid money and avoided the new certification, placement, and state-authorization requirements entirely.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: 2 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other senators joined.

against.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: Only Democratic senators supported it and no committee vote was ever taken, so no roll-call record shows how the parties would have split; the practical decision was made by a single committee chair of either party.

industries.note: These schools collect federal aid for licensure-prep programs that sometimes don't qualify graduates for the required exams or placements. The bill would strip their federal funding for such programs, which is why industry groups opposed similar protections when they were pursued through regulation.

The bill requires legal authorization in every state where enrolled students live, but it explicitly allows existing state reciprocity agreements to satisfy that requirement, so large online providers keep their current cross-state access while facing new documentation and complaint-process rules.

industries.industry: Accrediting agencies and state licensing boards
industries.note: The bill makes programmatic accreditation and state licensure prerequisites the gateway for federal aid eligibility, reinforcing their gatekeeping role over which programs students can fund with federal money.
